content:
Your LEFT JOIN might be an INNER JOIN in disguise.

If you filter the right table in WHERE, unmatched rows carry NULL, the condition fails, and those rows disappear. Move the filter into ON and every customer stays.

A small fix, but a big difference in reconciliation reports.

The problem

This query looks like it keeps every customer:

SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed';

It doesn’t. A customer with no orders gets NULL in every orders column. The WHERE clause then tests NULL = 'completed', which is not true, so the row is filtered out. Customers without a completed order vanish, and the result behaves like an INNER JOIN.

The fix

Move the filter into the ON clause:

SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
 AND o.status = 'completed';

Now the filter decides which orders match, instead of which rows survive. Every customer stays, and those without a completed order show NULL for the order columns.

Why it matters

Reconciliation reports depend on the left table staying complete. If customers disappear silently, totals look plausible but don’t match the source, and nobody gets an error. A simple check helps: compare the row count of your output against the left table, for example with a dbt test.

When WHERE is correct

  • Finding unmatched rows: WHERE o.order_id IS NULL is an anti-join, and the filter is intentional.
  • Wanting inner behavior: if you really want only customers with completed orders, write INNER JOIN, so the next reader doesn’t have to guess.

Save this for your next code review.
description: Filtering the right table in WHERE quietly turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN. Here is why it happens and the one-line fix.
title: Your LEFT JOIN Might Be an INNER JOIN in Disguise

content:
Learning Databricks and Spark joins, and still guessing why your job is slow? You don’t need a cluster to find out.

I built a local, hands-on walkthrough of how Spark executes a join, broadcast versus shuffle (sort-merge), using nothing but a laptop and PySpark in local mode. No Databricks, no cloud cluster, just the mechanics made visible.

The core idea

Spark has two fundamentally different ways to join data.

  • Broadcast join: Spark copies the small table to every executor, and each task does the match locally. There is no network shuffle, so it is nearly free.
  • Sort-merge join: Spark shuffles both sides across the cluster by key, sorts them, then merges. It moves your entire dataset across the wire.

Most people let Spark’s autoBroadcastJoinThreshold decide silently. That works until Spark guesses wrong on a table that isn’t actually small, and the job (or the driver) pays for it.

You can see which strategy Spark picked by reading the physical plan:

from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast

# Ask Spark to broadcast the small side
joined = big_df.join(broadcast(small_df), "key")

# The plan shows BroadcastHashJoin or SortMergeJoin
joined.explain()

Three things that became concrete

Working through this hands-on, a few ideas stopped being theory.

1. A broadcast join can’t preserve unmatched rows from the broadcast side

Spark scans one side row by row, while the other side is copied whole to every task. Because no single task ever sees the complete picture of the broadcast side, it can’t tell which of its rows went unmatched across the whole dataset. This isn’t a limitation to work around. It’s structural.

2. A broadcast hint on a join type that can’t support it is silently ignored

Put a broadcast hint on a join type that can’t use it, such as a full outer join, and your job doesn’t crash. Spark quietly ignores the hint and falls back to a shuffle. If you assumed you were getting a broadcast, you’d never know unless you checked the plan.

3. Skew doesn’t show up until you look

Say one key holds 30% of your rows. A sort-merge join’s “evenly split work” turns into one task doing most of the job while the rest finish early. Everything looks fine in the aggregate numbers, and the problem only appears when you inspect individual tasks.

Try it yourself

If this isn’t clear enough, the hands-on walkthrough is here: Spark joins walkthrough. Work through it yourself, and feel free to get in touch and tell me how your team decides between broadcast and shuffle in production.

Thanks to Narender Kumar, whose videos were a valuable source for this.
description: A local, hands-on walkthrough of broadcast and sort-merge joins in PySpark, with no cluster required.
title: How Spark Actually Executes a Join: Broadcast vs. Sort-Merge

Las ecuaciones matemáticas se pueden renderizar usando la sintaxis de Mathjax con soporte de símbolos AMS.

Opcionalmente, habilita esto por página agregando mathjax: true a tu frontmatter.

Luego, usa $$ ... $$ en una línea por sí sola para renderizar una ecuación de bloque:

$$ | Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{1}} [A(x) = 1] - Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{2}} [A(x) = 1] | < \text{negligible} $$

La versión sin procesar es:

$$ | Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{1}} [A(x) = 1] - Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{2}} [A(x) = 1] | < \text{negligible} $$

Escribe ecuaciones en línea con \\( ... \\) , como \( x^n / y \) . ¡Es fácil!

Los emoji se pueden habilitar en un proyecto Hugo de varias maneras. :zap:

Soporte de Emoji

La función emojify se puede llamar directamente en las plantillas o Shortcodes en línea.

Para habilitar emoji globalmente, establece enableEmoji en true en la configuración de tu sitio y luego puedes escribir códigos abreviados de emoji directamente en los archivos de contenido; por ejemplo:

La Hoja de trucos de Emoji es una referencia útil para los códigos abreviados de emoji.

N.B. Los pasos anteriores habilitan los caracteres y secuencias de emoji del Estándar Unicode en Hugo, sin embargo, la representación de estos glifos depende del navegador y la plataforma. Para estilizar los emoji, puedes usar una fuente de emoji de terceros o una pila de fuentes; por ejemplo:

.emoji {
  font-family: Apple Color Emoji, Segoe UI Emoji, NotoColorEmoji, Segoe UI Symbol, Android Emoji, EmojiSymbols;
}
title: Soporte de Emoji

content:
Les emoji peuvent être activés dans un projet Hugo de plusieurs façons. :zap:

Support des Emoji

La fonction emojify peut être appelée directement dans les modèles ou les Shortcodes en ligne.

Pour activer les emoji globalement, définissez enableEmoji sur true dans la configuration de votre site, puis vous pouvez taper les codes abrégés d’emoji directement dans les fichiers de contenu; par exemple :

La Feuille de triche Emoji est une référence utile pour les codes abrégés d’emoji.

N.B. Les étapes ci-dessus activent les caractères et séquences emoji du standard Unicode dans Hugo, cependant le rendu de ces glyphes dépend du navigateur et de la plateforme. Pour styliser les emoji, vous pouvez utiliser une police emoji tierce ou une pile de polices; par exemple :

.emoji {
  font-family: Apple Color Emoji, Segoe UI Emoji, NotoColorEmoji, Segoe UI Symbol, Android Emoji, EmojiSymbols;
}
title: Support des Emoji
